📌 Mark Price: Why Futures Can Be Liquidated Away From the Last Trade

Main Points
⏺ In futures trading, liquidation often depends on mark price, not the last traded price
⏺ Mark price helps protect traders from sharp manipulation and random wicks
⏺ This post explains why chart price and risk price can be different

1️⃣ Core Idea — mark price is calculated by the exchange using a model designed to reflect fairer market value.
2️⃣ Why It Exists — if positions were liquidated only by the last trade, one large order or thin order book could wipe traders out too easily.
3️⃣ Risk Surface — a trader may look at the last price and think the position is safe, while mark price is already close to liquidation.
4️⃣ What To Check — liquidation price, mark price, leverage, position size, and instrument volatility.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — in futures, don’t watch candles only; watch the position metrics inside the exchange interface.

Final Thoughts

Mark price is the price the exchange uses to measure position risk. If you trade with leverage, it can decide whether your position survives.

However, Bitcoin Staking alone cannot account for the entire 90 day rally on its own. Market conditions and renewed interest in the Stacks ecosystem have contributed to the price action as well. But unlike a short term price catalyst, the staking model creates a measurable link between institutional BTC participation and the amount of STX needed to support it.

➡️ The Genesis Bond has already put that relationship into practice, while Bond 2 and subsequent bonding periods will test whether it can repeat as more Bitcoin enters the program. Under Stacks’ Proof of Transfer system, miners commit BTC to compete for Stacks blocks and receive STX. The BTC committed through the process becomes the source of rewards distributed through the staking system.

⚠️ Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson has challenged Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin over his warning that advances in artificial intelligence could weaken quantum-resistant cryptography, arguing that existing security standards already account for decades of mathematical attacks. Hoskinson responded on October 9 to Buterin’s concerns about lattice-based cryptography, which is used in several modern security systems.
